verses.text: Who is like the wise man? Who knows the interpretation of a matter? A man's wisdom brightens his face, and the sternness of his face is changed.
Keep the king's command, I say, because of your oath before God.
Do not hasten to leave his presence, and do not persist in a bad cause, for he will do whatever he pleases.
For the king's word is supreme, and who can say to him, "What are you doing?"
Whoever keeps his command will come to no harm, and a wise heart knows the right time and procedure.
For there is a right time and procedure to every purpose, though a man's misery weighs heavily upon him.
Since no one knows what will happen, who can tell him what is to come?
As no man has power over the wind to contain it, so no one has authority over his day of death. As no one can be discharged in wartime, so wickedness will not release those who practice it.
All this I have seen, applying my mind to every deed that is done under the sun; there is a time when one man lords it over another to his own detriment.
Then too, I saw the burial of the wicked who used to go in and out of the holy place, and they were praised in the city where they had done so. This too is futile.
When the sentence for a crime is not speedily executed, the hearts of men become fully set on doing evil.
Although a sinner does evil a hundred times and still lives long, yet I also know that it will go well with those who fear God, who are reverent in His presence.
Yet because the wicked do not fear God, it will not go well with them, and their days will not lengthen like a shadow.

There is a futility that is done on the earth: There are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve, and there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve. I say that this too is futile.

So I commended the enjoyment of life, because there is nothing better for a man under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry. For this joy will accompany him in his labor during the days of his life that God gives him under the sun.
When I applied my mind to know wisdom and to observe the task that one performs on the earth—though his eyes do not see sleep in the day or even in the night—

I saw every work of God, and that a man is unable to comprehend the work that is done under the sun. Despite his efforts to search it out, he cannot find its meaning; even if the wise man claims to know, he is unable to comprehend.

context.author: “The Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem” (1:1); in Hebrew Qoheleth, “one who gathers” or “speaks to an assembly.” The book never names Solomon. Jewish and Christian tradition read it as Solomon; many scholars think a later writer took Solomon’s voice, because the Hebrew looks late and the speaker talks of kings before him in Jerusalem (1:16).
context.genre: Wisdom reflection: a searching first-person essay with poems and proverbs
context.audience: Anyone trying to find meaning in work, pleasure, wisdom and wealth, and finally “my son” (12:12)
context.setting: “A man’s wisdom brightens his face” (v.1). The Teacher advises caution at court: keep the king’s command because of your oath before God, and do not rush out of his presence, “for the king’s word is supreme” (vv.2-4). No one has power over the wind or over the day of his death (v.8). He has seen the wicked buried with honor (v.10), and “when the sentence for a crime is not speedily executed, the hearts of men become fully set on doing evil” (v.11). Even so, “I also know that it will go well with those who fear God” (v.12). Since the righteous sometimes get what the wicked deserve (v.14), he commends “the enjoyment of life” (v.15). No one, not even the wise, can comprehend the work of God (v.17).
context.custom: Servants of a king swore an oath of loyalty, often in the name of God (v.2). Soldiers could not be released in the middle of a war (v.8), though Deuteronomy 20:5-8 lists some who could go home before a battle. Funerals of important people passed through the city with great honor (v.10).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 9 says one fate comes to all, so eat your bread with joy and do whatever you do with all your might.
context.timelineBible: Paul tells believers to submit to rulers (Romans 13:1-7) and Peter to “honor the king” (1 Peter 2:17). Psalm 73 wrestles with the same puzzle of the prosperous wicked and the suffering righteous.

translation.meaning: King. The Teacher counsels wisdom and caution before a ruler.
Fearing, revering. It will go well with those who fear God.
Joy, gladness. The Teacher commends it as God’s gift for the days of toil.

gospelParallels.note: Be subject to the governing authorities.
The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise, but patient.

otBackground.note: Fear the LORD and the king.
Who may go home before battle.

overview.summary: Be wise before a king; no one controls the day of his death; justice is often delayed, yet it will go well with those who fear God, so enjoy life as God’s gift.
overview.settingLine: Advice for a servant at the king’s court.

history.t: Servants swore loyalty to the king.

customs.t: Do not rush out of the king’s presence.
The great were buried with honor.

archaeology.t: Assyrian treaty tablets made vassals swear loyalty to the king before the gods.
The kings of Judah were buried in the City of David (1 Kings 2:10).

overview.discussion: “When the sentence for a crime is not speedily executed, the hearts of men become fully set on doing evil” (v.11). How do I hold on to trust in God when justice is slow?
overview.book: The book of Ecclesiastes · 12 chapters. The Teacher searches for lasting gain “under the sun,” finds everything a breath, and ends: fear God and keep His commandments.
overview.author: The Teacher (Qoheleth)

peoplePlaces.d: It will go well with them

historicalImage.caption: The Visit of the Queen of Sheba to King Solomon, by Edward Poynter (1890, Art Gallery of New South Wales). The Teacher speaks as a king who had “silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces” (Ecclesiastes 2:8), the picture of Solomon’s court.
